items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the number of live births per 1000 population per year”.
items.answer: Crude birth rate
items.markingKey: Crude birth rate: the number of live births per 1000 population per year. [1]

items.stem: Explain why crude birth and death rates can be misleading when comparing countries.
items.answer: They are affected by age structure: a youthful population gives a low crude death rate even with poor health care, while an ageing population gives a high crude death rate despite good health; TFR and age-specific rates are better.
items.markingKey: 1 mark age structure; 1 mark example; 1 mark better measure [3]

items.stem: Describe the global pattern of total fertility rates.
items.answer: Highest in sub-Saharan Africa (e.g. Niger about 6), moderate in South Asia and parts of the Middle East, below replacement in Europe, East Asia (South Korea about 0.7), North America and much of Latin America.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per region with data [3]

items.stem: In one year Country R, with a mid-year population of 4.2 million, recorded 109 200 live births, 21 000 deaths and 7 644 deaths of infants under one year old. Suggest whether this country is an LIC or an HIC, using the data.
items.answer: Probably an LIC: high birth rate and high infant mortality.
items.markingKey: 1 mark judgement; 1 mark data [2]

items.stem: In one year Country Q, with a mid-year population of 4.2 million, recorded 130 200 live births, 46 200 deaths and 3 515 deaths of infants under one year old. (a) Calculate the rate of natural increase as a percentage. (b) Suggest whether this country is an LIC or an HIC, using the data.
items.answer: (a) +2% (b) Probably a middle-income country: indicators are intermediate or mixed.
items.markingKey: (a) (31 − 11) ÷ 10 [1] (b) 1 mark judgement; 1 mark data [2]

items.stem: In one year Country P, with a mid-year population of 4.2 million, recorded 163 800 live births, 46 200 deaths and 5 242 deaths of infants under one year old. (a) Calculate the crude birth rate and the crude death rate. (b) Suggest whether this country is an LIC or an HIC, using the data.
items.answer: (a) CBR 39 per 1000; CDR 11 per 1000 (b) Probably an LIC: high birth rate and high infant mortality.
items.markingKey: (a) births (deaths) ÷ population × 1000 [2] (b) 1 mark judgement; 1 mark data [2]

items.stem: Freya argues that the total fertility rate is the most useful measure of population change. How far do you agree? Support your answer with examples. In your answer you may refer to crude rates, age structure and population momentum.
items.answer: For: TFR is independent of age structure and predicts long-term growth; it allows comparison between countries (Niger about 6 v South Korea about 0.7). Against: Crude birth and death rates, infant mortality and life expectancy show other aspects; migration can dominate change (Gulf states); population momentum means TFR alone does not predict short-term change. Conclusion: TFR is the best single indicator of future natural change, but full understanding needs mortality, age structure and migration data.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “crude birth rate”?
options: The number of deaths of infants under one year old per 1000 live births per year.
The number of deaths per 1000 population per year.
The number of live births per 1000 population per year.
The average number of children a woman would have during her reproductive life (15-49) at current age-specific rates.
items.answer: The number of live births per 1000 population per year.
items.markingKey: Crude birth rate: the number of live births per 1000 population per year. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “A country with a fertility rate below 2.1 will start to lose population immediately.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Population momentum from a youthful age structure and immigration can keep the population growing for decades.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain why infant mortality rate is often used as an indicator of development.
items.answer: It reflects access to clean water, sanitation, maternal health care, nutrition and vaccination, so it is sensitive to living conditions.

items.answer: (a) Below replacement level (2.1): TFR = 1.69. (b) Low: female education and employment, cost of raising children, contraception, late marriage, urban lifestyles.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “social or religious values that encourage large families”.
items.answer: Pronatalist culture
items.markingKey: Pronatalist culture: social or religious values that encourage large families. [1]

items.stem: Explain the social and economic factors that keep fertility high in many LICs.
items.answer: Children work on farms and support parents in old age; high infant mortality; low female education and status; early marriage; limited access to contraception; religious and cultural values.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per factor explained [4]

items.stem: Explain why mortality rates have fallen in LICs since 1950.
items.answer: Vaccination programmes, antibiotics, clean water and sanitation, better nutrition, oral rehydration therapy, improved maternal care and education.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [3]

items.stem: A student tested the relationship between GNI per capita and infant mortality rate for 8 countries. Country 5: 41.4, 38. Country 6: 45.9, 36. Country 7: 55.2, 6. Country 8: 59.2, 2. Critical values of rs for n = 8: 0.643 (0.05 level) and 0.833 (0.01 level). Suggest one limitation of the method and how the investigation could be improved.
items.answer: National averages hide regional inequality; some countries achieve low IMR at modest incomes (Sri Lanka, Cuba); include more countries and other variables.
items.markingKey: 1 mark limitation; 1 mark improvement [2]

items.stem: A student collected data for 11 countries to test whether total fertility rate is related to female literacy. Table 4.3 gives, for each country, the female adult literacy rate (%) and the total fertility rate. Country 1: 25, 6.8. Country 2: 40, 6.4. Country 3: 69, 3.4. Country 4: 73, 3.9. Country 5: 74, 2.2. Country 6: 75, 4.2. Country 7: 79, 3.3. Country 8: 80, 3.7. Country 9: 92, 1.8. Country 10: 97, 1.2. Country 11: 99, 1.5. Critical values of rs for n = 11: 0.536 (0.05 level) and 0.709 (0.01 level). (a) State a suitable null hypothesis for this investigation. (b) Suggest one limitation of the method and how the investigation could be improved.
items.answer: (a) There is no relationship between the female adult literacy rate (%) and the total fertility rate. (b) Correlation does not prove causation: income, urbanisation and policy also vary; use more countries and control for income.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) 1 mark limitation; 1 mark improvement [2]

items.stem: Assess the view that the status of women is the most important influence on fertility. In your answer you may refer to infant mortality and education.
items.answer: For: Female education, employment and autonomy are strongly linked to lower TFR (Kerala, Bangladesh); women choose smaller families when they control decisions. Against: Infant mortality, income and urbanisation, religion and culture, government policy (China’s one-child policy) and access to family planning also influence fertility. Conclusion: The status of women is a key underlying factor, but its effect operates alongside mortality decline, economic change and policy.

items.stem: A student writes: “Economic development is the only cause of falling fertility.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Government policy (China, Iran), education, religion and access to contraception also matter, sometimes before significant development.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain why female education reduces fertility.
items.answer: Educated women marry later, have more knowledge of and access to contraception, enter paid employment (raising the opportunity cost of children), and have more say in family size; children are more likely to survive.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point [3]

items.answer: (a) There is no relationship between the female adult literacy rate (%) and the total fertility rate. (b) Literate women marry later, use contraception, work outside the home and have more control over family size; literacy is also linked to lower infant mortality.

items.stem: Explain the limitations of the dependency ratio.
items.answer: It assumes everyone aged 15-64 works and those outside it do not; many young people are in education, many older people work, unemployment and informal work are ignored; it does not show productivity.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point [3]

items.stem: Explain the impact of a youthful population structure on a country.
items.answer: Pressure on schools, health care and future jobs and housing; high youth dependency; possible demographic dividend if jobs are created; population momentum.

items.stem: With the help of examples, evaluate the claim that a youthful population structure brings more problems than opportunities. In your answer you may refer to education, employment and services.
items.answer: For: Pressure on schools, health care and housing; high youth unemployment and possible unrest; slow per capita growth (Niger, Uganda). Against: A demographic dividend if young people are educated and employed (East Asian growth, India today); large labour force attracts investment; future workers support an older generation. Conclusion: A youthful structure is a problem in the short term but can become an opportunity if investment in education and jobs is made.

items.stem: A student writes: “A high dependency ratio always means a country has many elderly people.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. In most LICs it is high because of many young dependants.

items.stem: Explain why females outnumber males in older age groups in most countries.
items.answer: Women have a higher life expectancy due to biological factors and lower rates of risky behaviour, occupational hazards, smoking and alcohol; war deaths affect men.

items.stem: In Doha, Qatar, the 25-29 age group contains 15 000 males and 11 900 females. Explain one consequence of an unbalanced sex ratio.
items.answer: Difficulty finding marriage partners; social problems; remittance-dependent households with absent men; changing roles of women.

items.stem: In Country A, with a total population of 30 million, 25% of people are aged 0-14, 64% are aged 15-64 and 11% are aged 65 and over. (a) Calculate the number of people aged 65 and over. (b) Explain two challenges this structure creates for the government.
items.answer: (a) 3.3 million (b) Creating enough jobs for a large working-age population; planning for future rapid ageing.
items.markingKey: (a) 11% of 30 million [1] (b) 1 mark each challenge with development [4]

items.stem: In Country A, with a total population of 12 million, 12% of people are aged 0-14, 66% are aged 15-64 and 22% are aged 65 and over. Describe the likely shape of the population pyramid.
items.answer: Narrow base, near-vertical sides and a wide top (beehive or inverted).

items.stem: In a mining town in Western Australia, the 0-4 age group contains 130 000 males and 132 000 females. (a) Calculate the sex ratio (males per 100 females). (b) Explain one consequence of an unbalanced sex ratio.
items.answer: (a) 98.5 (b) Difficulty finding marriage partners; social problems; remittance-dependent households with absent men; changing roles of women.
items.markingKey: (a) males ÷ females × 100 [1] (b) [2]

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that a youthful population structure brings more problems than opportunities? In your answer you may refer to education, demographic dividend and services.
items.answer: For: Pressure on schools, health care and housing; high youth unemployment and possible unrest; slow per capita growth (Niger, Uganda). Against: A demographic dividend if young people are educated and employed (East Asian growth, India today); large labour force attracts investment; future workers support an older generation. Conclusion: A youthful structure is a problem in the short term but can become an opportunity if investment in education and jobs is made.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the average number of children a woman would have during her reproductive life (15-49) at current age-specific rates”.
items.answer: Total fertility rate
items.markingKey: Total fertility rate: the average number of children a woman would have during her reproductive life (15-49) at current age-specific rates. [1]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) A revision website states: “Life expectancy has increased in almost all countries since 1950.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) A student writes: “A country with a fertility rate below 2.1 will start to lose population immediately.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Global life expectancy rose from about 46 years in 1950 to about 73 years by 2023. (b) Not correct. Population momentum from a youthful age structure and immigration can keep the population growing for decades.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) A revision website states: “Life expectancy has increased in almost all countries since 1950.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) In a class discussion, a student says: “The rate of natural increase ignores migration.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Global life expectancy rose from about 46 years in 1950 to about 73 years by 2023. (b) Correct. It only compares births and deaths; total change also includes net migration.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Table 10.2 shows age-specific fertility rates (births per 1000 women per year) for Country X: 15-19: 5, 20-24: 33, 25-29: 74, 30-34: 93, 35-39: 56, 40-44: 14, 45-49: 1. Identify the age group with the highest fertility and suggest a reason.
items.answer: 30-34: women delay childbirth because of education and careers, typical of HICs.
items.markingKey: 1 mark group; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: In one year Country S, with a mid-year population of 7.5 million, recorded 315 000 live births, 67 500 deaths and 17 955 deaths of infants under one year old. (a) Calculate the rate of natural increase as a percentage. (b) Estimate the doubling time of the population if natural increase continues at this rate.

In one year Country R, with a mid-year population of 4.2 million, recorded 138 600 live births, 42 000 deaths and 3 604 deaths of infants under one year old. (a) Calculate the crude birth rate and the crude death rate. (b) Suggest whether this country is an LIC or an HIC, using the data.
items.answer: (a) CBR 33 per 1000; CDR 10 per 1000 (b) Probably a middle-income country: indicators are intermediate or mixed.

items.stem: Table 10.2 shows age-specific fertility rates (births per 1000 women per year) for Country Z: 15-19: 66, 20-24: 219, 25-29: 219, 30-34: 175, 35-39: 110, 40-44: 44, 45-49: 11. (a) Identify the age group with the highest fertility and suggest a reason. (b) Suggest two reasons for the level of fertility shown.
items.answer: (a) 20-24: early marriage and childbearing, typical of LICs. (b) High: children as labour and old-age security, high infant mortality, limited contraception and female education, religious and cultural norms.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the number of women who die from pregnancy-related causes per 100 000 live births”.
items.answer: Maternal mortality ratio

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) In a class discussion, a student says: “In some HICs death rates are rising even though health care is improving.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain why mortality rates have fallen in LICs since 1950.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Ageing populations mean more elderly people, so crude death rates rise (e.g. Japan, Italy). (b) Vaccination programmes, antibiotics, clean water and sanitation, better nutrition, oral rehydration therapy, improved maternal care and education.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) 1 mark each [3]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) In a class discussion, a student says: “In some HICs death rates are rising even though health care is improving.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) A student writes: “Economic development is the only cause of falling fertility.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Ageing populations mean more elderly people, so crude death rates rise (e.g. Japan, Italy). (b) Not correct. Government policy (China, Iran), education, religion and access to contraception also matter, sometimes before significant development.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: A student collected data for 8 countries to test whether total fertility rate is related to female literacy. Table 3.1 gives, for each country, the female adult literacy rate (%) and the total fertility rate. Country 1: 23, 6.8. Country 2: 25, 5.9. Country 3: 26, 6.1. Country 4: 39, 5.2. Country 5: 45, 5.1. Country 6: 59, 2.9. Country 7: 73, 1.2. Country 8: 74, 1.5. Critical values of rs for n = 8: 0.643 (0.05 level) and 0.833 (0.01 level). Suggest one limitation of the method and how the investigation could be improved.
items.answer: Correlation does not prove causation: income, urbanisation and policy also vary; use more countries and control for income.
items.markingKey: 1 mark limitation; 1 mark improvement [2]

items.stem: A student collected data for 11 countries to test whether total fertility rate is related to female literacy. Table 4.3 gives, for each country, the female adult literacy rate (%) and the total fertility rate. Country 1: 27, 6.2. Country 2: 31, 5.3. Country 3: 33, 6.8. Country 4: 36, 5.1. Country 5: 52, 5.5. Country 6: 66, 4.3. Country 7: 73, 3.8. Country 8: 80, 3.2. Country 9: 91, 2.7. Country 10: 95, 2.3. Country 11: 96, 1.2. Critical values of rs for n = 11: 0.536 (0.05 level) and 0.709 (0.01 level). (a) State a suitable null hypothesis for this investigation. (b) Suggest one limitation of the method and how the investigation could be improved.
items.answer: (a) There is no relationship between the female adult literacy rate (%) and the total fertility rate. (b) Correlation does not prove causation: income, urbanisation and policy also vary; use more countries and control for income.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) 1 mark limitation; 1 mark improvement [2]

items.stem: “The status of women is the most important influence on fertility.” How far do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: For: Female education, employment and autonomy are strongly linked to lower TFR (Kerala, Bangladesh); women choose smaller families when they control decisions. Against: Infant mortality, income and urbanisation, religion and culture, government policy (China’s one-child policy) and access to family planning also influence fertility. Conclusion: The status of women is a key underlying factor, but its effect operates alongside mortality decline, economic change and policy.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “dependency ratio”?
options: The population aged 0-14 divided by the population aged 15-64, multiplied by 100.
The population aged 65 and over divided by the population aged 15-64, multiplied by 100.
The ratio of the dependent population (0-14 and 65+) to the economically active population (15-64), multiplied by 100.
The number of males per 100 females in a population.
items.answer: The ratio of the dependent population (0-14 and 65+) to the economically active population (15-64), multiplied by 100.

items.stem: A revision website states: “Migration can change the shape of a population pyramid.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Labour migration adds working-age males (Gulf states) and emigration removes them (rural Nepal).
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) In a class discussion, a student says: “Population pyramids can show the effects of past wars and policies.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain the limitations of the dependency ratio.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Indentations reveal low births or high deaths, e.g. the narrow cohorts born during China’s 1959-61 famine. (b) It assumes everyone aged 15-64 works and those outside it do not; many young people are in education, many older people work, unemployment and informal work are ignored; it does not show productivity.
